text: Why is it that printer ink costs more than champagne?
You need to print one page. One. A boarding pass, maybe a contract you'll sign and never read.
You press print. And the printer tells you it's out of cyan.
You're printing in black and white.
Let's start with the numbers. Measured per milliliter, the ink in many home printer cartridges costs more than vintage champagne. More than many luxury perfumes.
Consumer groups have compared it to some of the most expensive liquids you can legally buy.
And here's the thing. Ink isn't rare. It's mostly water, some pigment or dye, and a few chemicals to keep it from drying out.
So why does a few milliliters of colored water cost more than your weekly groceries?
To understand printers, you have to understand razors. It's called the razor-and-blades model.
You sell the razor cheap, maybe even at a loss. Then you make your money on the blades, which the customer has to buy again and again. Forever.
Printer companies took this idea and perfected it.
That printer you bought for fifty bucks? The manufacturer may barely break even on it. Sometimes they lose money. They don't care.
Because the printer isn't the product. You are.
And it gets better. Many new printers ship with so-called starter cartridges. They look exactly like the real ones. They just contain less ink. Sometimes a lot less.
So the first time you run out, it's sooner than you expected. Which is, coincidentally, exactly when you start buying cartridges. Pure coincidence. Absolutely.
Now, you might think: fine, I'll just buy cheaper ink from another brand. The printer companies thought of that too.
Modern cartridges often contain a small chip. Officially, it tracks ink levels and helps with print quality. Unofficially, it lets the printer check whether the cartridge is genuine.
If it isn't, the printer might reject it. Or show warnings. Or simply refuse to work.
In some cases, printers that worked perfectly fine with cheaper cartridges suddenly stopped after a firmware update. A software update. That made your printer worse. On purpose.
This led to lawsuits, settlements, and a lot of very angry people on the internet. Which, to be fair, is the internet's natural state.
Some all-in-one printers have even been accused of refusing to scan when the ink is low. Scanning. Which uses zero ink.
That's like your car refusing to play the radio because you're low on fuel.
And now we've entered the final form: ink subscriptions. You pay monthly. The printer tells the company when it's running low. New ink arrives by mail. Convenient!
Until you cancel. And the ink you already have in your printer may stop working. Because technically, you never owned it. You were renting colored water.
So why does this keep working? Because we buy printers based on the price on the box, not the price of the next five years.
And once you own one, switching feels like more effort than just buying another cartridge. It's not a bad product. It's a brilliant trap.

There is hope. Ink tank printers cost more upfront, but you refill them from bottles that last a very long time. Laser printers use toner, which is far cheaper per page. And honestly? For a lot of people, the best printer is the one at the library.
The real lesson is simple: when something is suspiciously cheap, ask where the money is actually coming from.
So next time your printer says it's out of cyan while you're printing in black and white, remember. It's not broken. It's working exactly as intended.
Why is it that... you haven't subscribed yet?
